playbook:
I track my real budget from the stated starting amount minus lots I have actually won, and I report that true figure in the budget token. A bid I have placed but not yet won does not reduce my budget — if it is topped or the lot closes against me, I still have that cash. Lying about my budget in either direction costs me.

I never bid more than my real remaining budget, and never above the lot's value to me. If the minimum raise exceeds either, I pass immediately.

I do not spend my entire budget on one lot, even a high-margin one. Winning lot 2 at 30 left me with 0 to fight for lots worth 30 and 36 that went for 16 and 8. Total surplus available was far larger than the 5 I got. I cap any single bid at a fraction of my budget unless it is the last lot.

My surplus price target on a lot is value minus a healthy margin, not value minus nothing. Winning at 30 for a 35-value lot yields 5; winning at 12 for a 25-value lot yields 13. Cheap wins beat maximum wins.

My bid in a round is not final — rivals can still top it. So on a lot I want, I bid near my price target immediately rather than dribbling up; a token low bid just invites raises.

I prioritize: compute (value − likely winning price) for every remaining lot and spread real bids across the top few margins rather than dumping everything into the first good lot. Close wins are often available because rivals show restraint — lots here went at 8, 16, 16 even with values in the 30s.

On lots worth less than their estimate, or below later lots' margins, I pass cheaply and preserve cash — unless the standing price is so low relative to value (e.g. 8 for a 25-value lot, final round) that a single mid-range bid likely wins with fat margin. Passing lot 1 entirely when 12 could plausibly have won a 25-value lot was leaving surplus on the table.

On the last lot, leftover budget is worthless, so I bid as much of it as the lot's value justifies — but never past value. Before doing this I make sure I actually still have budget: if I find myself at 0 for the final lots, I spent too aggressively earlier.

Before submitting, I verify: bid ≥ standing high + minimum raise, bid ≤ value, bid ≤ true remaining budget, planned purchases across remaining lots fit my budget, and the budget token equals true cash currently in hand.

I keep the reply short and always end with both required tokens.

1.text:
The biggest correction from this episode: round 2 is NOT my last word. I assumed a final-round minimal bid locks the win, but rivals act after me within the round — lot 1 (I bid 12, rival won at 16) and lot 4 (I bid 6, rival won at 8) both got stolen for a token raise over my minimal bid. I left two lots worth 71 combined on the table over a few extra dollars. From now on, minimal final-round topping is off the table unless my value or budget genuinely forbids more.

Round 2 policy, revised: I bid as high as my constraints allow, to make counter-bidding expensive for rivals. My bid = min(my value, my remaining budget). Bidding full value caps my surplus at zero, but a zero-surplus win is worth as much as losing at zero, and it forces any rival to actually overpay to take the lot. Exception: if standing + minimum raise is already near my value (small headroom) and rivals in this episode have shown they counter, bidding full value is fine; if rivals have shown they DON'T counter round-2 bids (losses recorded at exactly my bid or thereabouts), I can go back to standing + raise and keep the surplus. Default to the aggressive version — observed rivals do counter.

Also on final-round bids: whether I want to exclude a rival cheaply depends on what that rival's observed final prices look like. When rivals consistently pay roughly estimate or their apparent value, bidding just below/at my own value is a strong deterrent; the experiment "they paid 16 for lot 1 and 8 for lot 4" shows they bid close to or above value, so deterring them requires real money, not minimal raises.

Round 1 stays cheap: minimum raise, since another round follows and I've won lots cheaply by saving my serious bid for round 2. But I note the standing bid in round 2 can already be large (lot 2 opened at 30 against my budget of 30 — unaffordable regardless of value). On early lots with a tight budget, I should not expect to win every lot; I pick battles.

Budget-token discipline: this episode it worked — I recomputed from the results list (won lot 3 at 16, starting 30 → 14) and tracked it correctly through lots 4 and 5. Keep doing exactly that: budget = starting amount minus amounts actually paid for lots I won, recomputed each turn from "Results so far," never from what I bid.

Binding constraint on every bid: min(remaining budget, value). Never more than I can pay. If the minimum legal raise exceeds my remaining budget, I pass immediately (lot 2 round 2 was handled correctly this way).

Prioritization with tight budget: commit to lots where (my value − current standing bid) is largest relative to price; that's where surplus per dollar is best. Don't spread thin. Lot 3 (won 16 for a 53-value lot) was the model outcome; earlier cheap-theft losses showed what playing too timidly costs.

I pass immediately when the standing bid already meets or exceeds my value — winning there locks in zero or negative surplus.

I bid against value and budget, not against the estimate, and I use observed rival behavior only for the two documented calibrations: whether rivals counter round-2 bids, and whether they overpay.

Replies stay short; I always end with both bracketed tokens, compute first, budget line last.

2.text:
- First thing at the table: I lock in my actual starting budget from the setup line and recompute remaining budget after every lot as start minus the sum of my winning bids shown in the results. I made the same [budget: 100] mistake again this episode when the start was 30 — the cross-check is mandatory, not aspirational: before submitting, the budget token must equal starting budget minus my wins listed in "results so far," and I say that arithmetic out loud in my reply note.

- When the standing high bid plus the minimum raise is below my value, I bid the minimum legal amount on low-to-medium value lots. Cheap tags conserve cash and cost nothing if a rival blows past.

- Exception, new this episode: on lots with a large surplus (my value far above the current bid, like lot 3 worth 42 when the lead was 8), I do not just tag the minimum and walk away. With only 2 rounds, minimum tags are easy for rivals to top, and I lost a huge-surplus lot for want of a few more. On high-value lots I stay engaged through round 2, raising by the minimum each time as long as the new required bid leaves a solid margin below my value.

- When the standing high bid already meets or exceeds my value, or the required raise would push past it, I pass unconditionally. Paying above value guarantees negative score. Lot 2 round 2 (bid 30 vs value 15): correct pass.

- When I am already the standing high bidder in the final round, I pass. Never raise myself.

- In round 2 I re-evaluate only against the new high bid, never anchoring on my round-1 bid: minimum raise if comfortably below value, pass otherwise.

- Rivals here jumped from tiny openers to bids at or above estimate (30 on a value-15 lot). Against overpayers I do not chase into their range — a rival paying double value is subsidizing me. But I distinguish "can't win cheaply" (pass) from "win cheaply with one more minimum raise" (stay in, per the high-surplus rule).

- Before bidding on the last two lots I explicitly check remaining budget and prioritize the lot with the biggest value-minus-winning-price surplus; if I can't afford both, I spend on the larger surplus. This episode the budget forced the choice for me — keep it deliberate.

- On the final lot, if the minimum winning bid fits my remaining budget and is below my value, I bid it even for tiny surplus — unspent budget scores nothing. Lot 5 round 2: required 8 against budget 6, so the pass was forced; verify affordability before passing, not after.

- Two-round lots mean round 1 is cheap information. I use round 1 to take the lead at minimum on anything below value, then decide for real money in round 2.

- I ignore estimates except as a weak hint about rivals; only my value, the standing bid, and my remaining budget drive decisions.

- Final pre-submit checklist every reply: (1) bid ≤ my value minus required margin? (2) bid ≤ remaining budget? (3) budget token = start − listed wins? State each number once in the note.
